title: A Autopsy for the Will
premise: Hazel Ashgrove, an insurance investigator with a photographic memory, is sent to close the file on Marlowe Vane, a woman declared dead seven years ago — until Hazel discovers Marlowe's diary contains entries written after her supposed death, in handwriting that matches her own late sister's. As Hazel follows the diary's coded trail through a coastal town that has agreed to forget, she uncovers a ring of townspeople who faked Marlowe's death to hide her from an abusive husband the law failed to convict. The final entry predicts Hazel's own arrival, forcing her to choose between exposing a justice that worked outside the law and protecting the found family that built it — a choice that ends with Hazel burning the official file and adding her own entry to the diary.
about_author: E. M. Lockridge is the pen name of a former claims adjuster who spent eleven years investigating deaths that never quite added up before turning to fiction full-time. They write from a house overlooking the Atlantic, where they insist every mystery must end with mercy or it isn't worth telling.

chapters.title: The File That Wouldn't Close
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Assigned to audit the cold-case payout on Marlowe Vane's death, Hazel notices the coroner's report contradicts itself in three places only her memory would catch. The emotional beat is professional unease hardening into obsession — the first crack in a case everyone else calls shut.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. In the evidence box, Hazel finds Marlowe's diary and reads entries dated weeks after the recorded drowning, including one describing 'the investigator with the perfect memory' — Hazel herself. Shock gives way to vertigo; the case was never about a death but a disappearance staged to be found.

chapters.title: Saltburn Point
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She travels to the fog-bound fishing town where Marlowe vanished and finds a community that answers questions with rehearsed sameness, word for word, as if coached. The beat is isolation — Hazel realizes the whole town may be lying in unison, and that she's being watched.

chapters.title: The Widow Who Isn't Grieving
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel interviews Grant Vane, Marlowe's husband, a charming philanthropist whose alibi for the night of the drowning is flawless because he wrote it himself — Hazel recognizes recycled phrasing from his earlier statements. Cold dread: this man has practiced innocence for years.

chapters.title: A Room Full of Sisters
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. At the harbor diner, Hazel meets Odessa Pike, the cook who once employed Marlowe, and feels an instant, unearned kinship — the first warmth since her sister's death. Odessa slips her a matchbook with a phone number and one whispered word: 'Thursday.'

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Following the diary's tide-table cipher, Hazel searches a sea cave at low tide and finds a hidden cache: cash, false papers, and a second diary — her own sister's handwriting, proving her sister helped stage Marlowe's escape before dying herself. Grief and fury collide.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Thursdays
chapters.summary: Odessa's POV. Flashback chapter: Odessa recounts how the town's women built the network that hid Marlowe after the courts dismissed her abuse case, meeting every Thursday for seven years to pass messages along a chain of safe houses. The beat is fierce tenderness — justice as domestic labor.

chapters.title: The Man Who Counts Doors
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Grant Vane invites Hazel to dinner and demonstrates, pleasantly, that he knows exactly which rooms she's rented, which calls she's made, which doors she's opened. The emotional beat is claustrophobic menace delivered with impeccable manners.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Someone torches the cave cache hours after Hazel leaves it, and the police chief — a Thursday regular, she now suspects — warns her off in language that is half threat, half plea. Hazel must decide whether the town protecting Marlowe just tried to destroy her evidence.

chapters.title: The Chain of Hands
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Decoding the diary's route, Hazel maps the safe-house chain and realizes each link was a woman who lost something to the legal system — a daughter returned to an abuser, a case thrown out, a testimony disbelieved. The beat is recognition: this is what justice looks like when law fails.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Firelight
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The Thursday circle finally summons Hazel and interrogates her motives over a driftwood fire: is she law, insurance, or family? Hazel confesses her sister's role and her own hunger for a verdict no court ever gave. Trust is extended like a blade, handle first.

chapters.title: Marlowe, Alive
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. Hazel meets the living Marlowe Vane in a lighthouse keeper's cottage — weathered, watchful, unrepentant. Marlowe explains why the diary had to surface now: Grant has remarried, and history is repeating with a new wife named Corinne. The beat is moral gravity passed like a weight.

chapters.title: Corinne
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel tracks Corinne Vane, twenty-six, newly isolated, credit cards monitored, friends warned away — the same pattern, seven years later. Fear sharpens into urgency: whatever the town decides, there is a living woman in danger right now.

chapters.title: The Insurance Man's Ledger
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Using actuarial records only her memory can cross-reference, Hazel proves Grant profited from two prior 'accidental' deaths — a business partner, a first fiancée — deaths ruled misadventure. The beat is cold triumph curdling into horror at the scale of it.

chapters.title: A Vote Among Thieves of Grief
chapters.summary: Odessa's POV. The Thursday circle votes on whether to help Hazel take Grant down or simply move Corinne and vanish deeper. Old wounds split the women; Odessa casts the deciding vote for confrontation, knowing some of them may pay for it. The beat is solidarity strained to breaking.

chapters.title: The Trap Wears a Wedding Ring
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The plan: bait Grant with evidence that Marlowe is alive and reachable, drawing him to the lighthouse on the anniversary of the drowning. Hazel plays the messenger, terrified and certain, aware she is offering herself as proof of life.

chapters.title: Anniversary Fog
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Grant takes the bait but arrives early and armed, trapping Hazel alone in the lighthouse; he confesses everything with the calm of a man narrating his own biography. The beat is terror transmuted into clarity — Hazel memorizes every word, her memory now the only witness that matters.

chapters.title: What Memory Is For
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Cornered at the lantern room's rail, Hazel stalls Grant while the Thursday women converge through the fog; Marlowe steps out of the dark, alive, and Grant's certainty shatters. The confession spills before witnesses, tape recorders, and the one thing he cannot charm: the truth spoken aloud.

chapters.title: The Verdict Outside the Courtroom
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Grant is arrested on evidence Hazel reconstructed from memory — but the town refuses to celebrate, because the law that failed Marlowe will now try her for fraud. The beat is bittersweet victory: justice arrives, imperfect and double-edged.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. On the stand, Hazel recites Grant's confession verbatim, dates and phrasings intact, unshakable under cross-examination; her photographic memory, once a party trick, becomes an instrument of reckoning. The beat is quiet power — the body itself as archive.

chapters.title: Sentencing the Living
chapters.summary: Marlowe's POV. Marlowe accepts a plea and community service rather than prison, the judge acknowledging the failure that preceded her crime; the Thursday circle absorbs her back without ceremony. The beat is grace without absolution — the town keeps its secrets and its people.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Months later, Hazel burns the official file, resigns from the firm, and writes her own entry in Marlowe's diary before passing it down the chain to the next woman who needs it. The beat is homecoming: Hazel, orphaned by blood, joins the family that justice built.
